The incidence of fatal accidents in underground mining was over three times the rate in surface mining, while the incidence of disabling accidents was almost 16 times greater in underground mines. Accidents involving machinery caused most fatalities in surface mining. For the first nine months of 1975, there were no fatal surface coal mine accidents in Montana and the nonfatal accident rate was 0.89 per million tons mined.
The railroad would pose some risk of accidents, but this risk should be fairly low because the trains are loaded continuously and remotely, and the train is not broken or switched during normal loading. Personnel are protected in the engine cab or crew car of the train. The only exposure from switching operations would be in moving equipment or supply cars onto sidings.
Population Related - Probably the greatest risk to mine employees would be during the daily commuting to and from the mine site. Based on 1974 figures from the Montana State Highway Department and assuming that a production workforce of 210 employees would commute from Hardin daily, There would be an estimated risk of 1 fatal accident every 5 years and 5 to 6 injuries per year for the next few years.
Archaeological Sites
While no significant and important historical Indian sites are known to exist in the Sarpy area, the inventoried sites do have some value as part of the human heritage. Those sites present on proposed mining areas will be lost unless further surveys uncover sites of sufficient significance to merit their protection.
